guide.title: Midwood, Brooklyn: Vitagraph, Fiske Terrace and Avenue J
guide.intro: The name comes from the Middle Dutch Midwout, middle woods, for the dense woodland between the Dutch towns of Bushwick and Breuckelen. Dutch settlement began around 1652, when Jan Snedeker, Jan Stryker and Tomys Swartwout petitioned Director-General Peter Stuyvesant for the right to settle; in April 1655 Stuyvesant and the Council of New Netherland appointed Swartwout a schepen, a magistrate, on the Court of Midwout. The area stayed rural after the English took control in 1664 and remained largely undeveloped until annexation into the City of Brooklyn in the 1890s, with dense middle-class building only accelerating in the 1920s. In between came the film industry: Vitagraph Studios put up a plant here in 1906, and Warner Bros. bought the company in 1925 and made sound shorts on the site until 1940.

sections.heading: Vitagraph, Fiske Terrace and the synagogues
sections.body:
Vitagraph Studios built what is described as the first modern film studio in the United States here in 1906, on a site whose edges were Locust Avenue, East 15th Street, Elm Avenue and the right-of-way of the BMT Brighton Line. Warner Bros. acquired Vitagraph on April 20, 1925, renamed the site Vitaphone and produced sound shorts there until it closed in 1940. The Landmarks Preservation Commission declined to designate the building in 2008, citing the loss of its original architectural features, and it was demolished in 2015 for apartments. Only the smokestack still stands.

The residential grid has a landmarked piece of its own. The Fiske Terrace-Midwood Park Historic District, designated on March 18, 2008, covers roughly 250 houses developed from 1905 onward by the T. B. Ackerson Company; Wikipedia notes Ackerson personally built about 150 of them. Its boundaries are given as Foster Avenue, Ocean Avenue, the LIRR Bay Ridge Branch right-of-way and the BMT Brighton Line corridor, and it sits on the Midwood and Flatbush line.

Two synagogues on the National Register mark the neighborhood's twentieth-century Jewish population. The East Midwood Jewish Center at 1625 Ocean Avenue was founded in 1924 by the dentist Jacob R. Schwartz; its Renaissance Revival building was completed in 1929 and listed on June 7, 2006 under reference number 06000478. The Kingsway Jewish Center at 2810 Nostrand Avenue was established as a congregation in 1928, and its Art Deco building of 1951, with eighteen windows by the artist Adolph Gottlieb, was listed on February 12, 2010 under reference number 10000010.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Two subway lines run through the neighborhood. On the BMT Brighton Line, Avenue J and Avenue M are Midwood stations served by the Q. Kings Highway, on the border of Midwood and Homecrest, is served by the Q at all times and the B on weekdays. Avenue H, on the border of Midwood and Flatbush near Fiske Terrace, is served by the Q, and its northbound station house is an individual city landmark.

On the IND Culver Line, Avenue I is a Midwood station, bordering Mapleton, served by the F at all times with peak-direction express service. Avenue N, described as spanning Bensonhurst, Mapleton and Midwood, has the same service.

Flatbush Avenue-Brooklyn College, on the IRT Nostrand Avenue Line, sits at The Junction in Flatbush and is described as bordering Midwood to the southwest; it is served by the 2 and the 5.

faq.question: How do I get to Midwood?
faq.answer: By subway. The Q calls at Avenue J, Avenue M, Kings Highway and Avenue H on the BMT Brighton Line, with the B also serving Kings Highway on weekdays. The F calls at Avenue I and Avenue N on the IND Culver Line. Flatbush Avenue-Brooklyn College, on the 2 and 5, sits at The Junction in Flatbush and borders Midwood to the southwest.

faq.question: Where does the name Midwood come from?
faq.answer: From the Middle Dutch Midwout, meaning middle woods. It described the dense woodland between the Dutch towns of Bushwick and Breuckelen, and Dutch settlement of the area began around 1652.

faq.question: Is anything left of Vitagraph Studios?
faq.answer: Only the smokestack. The Landmarks Preservation Commission declined to landmark the building in 2008, and the studio was demolished in 2015 for residential apartments. The smokestack stands near East 14th Street and Avenue M and is visible from the BMT Brighton Line.

faq.question: Is Di Fara Pizza still open?
faq.answer: Yes. Domenico DeMarco opened it at 1424 Avenue J in 1965 and it has continued under new ownership since his death in March 2022. Its commonly cited website returns a certificate error, so no official link is given here.

faq.question: Are there hotels in Midwood?
faq.answer: The research for this guide found no hotels or other lodging within Midwood, so none are listed rather than borrowing one from a neighbouring neighborhood.

places.name: Fiske Terrace-Midwood Park Historic District
places.address: Foster Avenue, Ocean Avenue, the LIRR Bay Ridge Branch right-of-way and the BMT Brighton Line corridor, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A New York City historic district covering roughly 250 early-1900s houses developed by the T. B. Ackerson Company from 1905 onward. It sits on the Midwood and Flatbush line.
places.history: Designated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission on March 18, 2008. Wikipedia notes that Ackerson personally built about 150 of the district's 250 designated houses, with others built by different developers.

places.name: Avenue H Station House
places.address: Avenue H and East 16th Street, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: The northbound station house on the BMT Brighton Line, built in 1906 by the T. B. Ackerson Company as a real estate sales office for the Fiske Terrace development and later converted for subway use. It is described as the only structure in the subway system not originally built as a transit facility.
places.history: The Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the exterior an individual landmark on June 29, 2004. It still functions as the working station entrance.

places.name: East Midwood Jewish Center
places.summary: A Conservative synagogue founded in 1924 by the dentist Jacob R. Schwartz. Its Renaissance Revival building was completed in 1929 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 7, 2006, reference number 06000478.

places.name: Kingsway Jewish Center
places.summary: A Modern Orthodox synagogue whose congregation was established in 1928. The Art Deco building was completed in 1951 with eighteen windows by the artist Adolph Gottlieb, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on February 12, 2010, reference number 10000010.

places.name: Vitagraph Studios Smokestack
places.address: Near East 14th Street and Avenue M, Brooklyn, NY, visible from the BMT Brighton Line
places.summary: The lone surviving structure of the Vitagraph and Vitaphone film studio complex, built in 1906. The Landmarks Preservation Commission declined to landmark the studio building in 2008 and it was demolished in 2015; the smokestack remains standing.

places.name: Kolbert Playground
places.address: 1706 Avenue L, between East 17th and East 18th Streets, Brooklyn, NY 11230
places.summary: A 1.58-acre NYC Parks playground named for a fallen World War II soldier. The city acquired the site in 1936, and NYC Parks lists it under Brooklyn Community Board 14.

places.name: Friends Field
places.address: Avenue L, East 4th Street, McDonald Avenue and Avenue M, Brooklyn, NY 11230
places.summary: A 6.7-acre park on land the Society of Friends bought in 1921 for Quaker-school athletics. NYC Parks acquired it on January 17, 1973, and lists it under Community Board 12 rather than Midwood's own Community Board 14.

places.name: Sgt. Joyce Kilmer Triangle
places.address: East 12th Street, Kings Highway and Quentin Road, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A 0.001-acre triangle named for Sgt. Joyce Kilmer, acquired as parkland on July 20, 1934. NYC Parks lists it under Community Board 15 rather than Midwood's Community Board 14.

places.name: Di Fara Pizza
places.summary: A pizzeria opened in 1965 by Domenico DeMarco, an immigrant from Italy's Caserta province. It has continued under new ownership since DeMarco's death in March 2022.

entries.name: Fiske Terrace-Midwood Park Historic District
entries.note: Roughly 250 houses built from 1905 by the T. B. Ackerson Company, landmarked in March 2008.

entries.name: Avenue H Station House
entries.note: A 1906 real estate sales office that became a subway entrance, and is still the working one.

entries.name: East Midwood Jewish Center
entries.note: A Renaissance Revival synagogue completed in 1929 for a congregation founded five years earlier.

entries.name: Kingsway Jewish Center
entries.note: An Art Deco synagogue of 1951 whose eighteen windows were made by the artist Adolph Gottlieb.

entries.name: Vitagraph Studios Smokestack
entries.note: All that is left of the 1906 studio, visible from the Brighton Line after the 2015 demolition.

entries.name: Kolbert Playground
entries.note: A 1.58-acre playground on Avenue L, in city hands since 1936 and named for a fallen soldier.

entries.name: Friends Field
entries.note: Nearly seven acres bought by the Society of Friends in 1921 and taken over by NYC Parks in 1973.

entries.name: Sgt. Joyce Kilmer Triangle
entries.note: A thousandth of an acre at Kings Highway and Quentin Road, parkland since July 1934.

entries.name: Di Fara Pizza
entries.note: On Avenue J since 1965, opened by Domenico DeMarco and carried on by new owners since 2022.

links.note: Avenue H on the Q sits on the Midwood and Flatbush border, and the Fiske Terrace-Midwood Park Historic District sits on the same line.
NYC Parks lists Friends Field under Community Board 12, the district that also covers most of Kensington.
The freight-only LIRR Bay Ridge Branch, given as Farragut's southern edge, also bounds the Fiske Terrace-Midwood Park Historic District.
